### Project Brief

In this project, I had the opportunity to explore Boston’s rapid transit system, known as the “T,” as a vital component of the city’s public transportation network. Using machine learning models and optimizing accuracy and minimizing errors, I used data analysis to make policy recommendations and aswer questions like do households value transit-rich neighborhoods compared to others? How certain can planners be about data-driven conclusions given some spatial biases?

This policy brief attempts to address the value and citzen settlement patterns of transit-rich neighborhoods, comparing them to the city at large. It makes extensive use of the American Community Survey data, along with publically available information on the MBTA’s rapid transit routes and stops.

      <p>Planners treat half a mile, about a ten-minute walk, as a station’s reach. These are the half-mile walksheds around the <span data-fill="stations">121</span> rapid transit stops in Suffolk County, which takes in Boston, Chelsea, Revere and Winthrop.</p>

    <article class="tod-step" data-step="tod">

      <p>A census tract counts as transit-oriented when its center falls inside a walkshed: <span data-fill="todTracts">136</span> of the county’s <span data-fill="tracts">234</span> tracts in 2020.</p>

    <article class="tod-step" data-step="income">

      <p>Median household income in transit-rich tracts rose from <span data-fill="incomeTod2016">$68,658</span> to <span data-fill="incomeTod2020">$82,324</span> in 2020 dollars, and the gap with the rest of the county widened.</p>
      <div data-compare="income"></div>
      <p class="live-source">*2016 values in 2020 dollars.</p>
    </article>
    <article class="tod-step" data-step="burden">
      <p class="live-eyebrow">Rent burden</p>
      <h3>Rent burden eased, but only near the T</h3>
      <p>Households that spend more than 30% of their income on rent are rent-burdened. The typical share in transit-rich tracts fell from <span data-fill="burdenTod2016">31.4%</span> to <span data-fill="burdenTod2020">30.4%</span> while it edged up elsewhere. Rents rose too, so the likelier story is higher-income households moving in, not housing getting cheaper.</p>
      <div data-compare="burden"></div>

    <article class="tod-step" data-step="close">

      <h3>Where TOD has to work hardest</h3>
      <p>Transit-rich neighborhoods are where Boston’s housing demand concentrates. Keeping homes near the T within reach of the people who rely on it most is where transit-oriented development has to work hardest.</p>
